narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 50.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The three factors that mattered most to the decision were your LSAT score, your first-year grades, and your family income. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and worked in your favor: at 34 it was only a few points below the average of 37 among accepted students, which helped push the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, your first-year grades pulled strongly in the opposite direction. Placing in the third decile is well below the average of sixth decile among accepted students, and this low ranking was the main reason the model saw a higher risk of failure. Your family’s upper-middle income level added a smaller additional push toward denial; while this bracket is common among accepted students, the model still associated it with slightly higher risk in your particular combination of academics.

In short, although your LSAT provided some positive momentum, your early law-school grades created the decisive drag that led to rejection.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance in the coming year. Raising your grades in the next semesters can directly counteract the negative signal from your first-year record and give you a much stronger application if you choose to reapply.
